flashcards.a: Responses had to return in request order (spec requirement), so one slow response head-of-line-blocked every faster response behind it, and real-world middlebox/proxy bugs mishandled pipelined traffic. No major browser shipped it enabled; Firefox removed the code entirely in v54 (2017).

flashcards.q: What workaround did browsers use for HTTP/1.1 HOL blocking, and what did it cost?
flashcards.a: 6 parallel TCP connections per origin (some browsers historically 2-8). Cost: 6x TCP handshakes, 6x TLS handshakes, 6x slow-start ramp-up, 6x server-side connection resources -- and each connection is still independently HOL-blocked.

flashcards.q: What are HTTP/2's two HPACK tables and their sizes?
flashcards.a: A static table of 61 predefined common header field name/value pairs, plus a per-connection dynamic table (default max size 4096 bytes) populated as headers are actually sent, so repeated headers (cookies, bearer tokens) are referenced by a 1-2 byte index instead of resent in full.

flashcards.q: What is HTTP/2's transport-layer HOL blocking gotcha?
flashcards.a: TCP delivers one ordered byte stream for the whole connection with no concept of 'stream.' One lost TCP segment stalls ALL multiplexed HTTP/2 streams behind it in the receive buffer, even ones unrelated to the loss -- can make HTTP/2 worse than 6 HTTP/1.1 connections on lossy (cellular) networks.

flashcards.q: Why did HTTP/2 server push die?
flashcards.a: The server can't know what the client already has cached, so naive push implementations re-pushed already-cached assets, wasting bandwidth in practice rather than saving a round trip. Chrome disabled it by default in Chrome 106 (October 2022) after data showed low adoption and no consistent win.

flashcards.q: What replaced HTTP/2 server push, and why is it safer?
flashcards.a: 103 Early Hints (RFC 8297): server sends an informational 103 response with Link/preload headers while still computing the real response, letting the client start fetching based on its OWN cache state -- avoiding push's cache-pollution failure mode.

flashcards.q: What transport does HTTP/3 run on, and why not just patch TCP instead?
flashcards.a: QUIC, built on UDP (RFC 9000/9114). TCP can't be evolved at the transport layer because it's baked into kernels and middleboxes across the whole internet (protocol ossification); QUIC sidesteps this by encrypting almost the entire packet so middleboxes can't meddle with it, and runs in userspace.

flashcards.q: How does QUIC solve transport-layer HOL blocking?
flashcards.a: Each QUIC stream has its own independent sequence space and loss-recovery/ack state (unlike TCP's single ordered byte stream for the whole connection). A lost UDP packet belongs to exactly one stream; only that stream stalls, others keep delivering immediately.

flashcards.q: Compare RTT cost for a fresh connection: TCP+TLS1.2 vs TCP+TLS1.3 vs QUIC.
flashcards.a: TCP+TLS1.2 ~3 RTT before app data flows. TCP+TLS1.3 collapses to ~2 RTT. QUIC integrates the handshake to ~1 RTT for a new connection, with 0-RTT resumption for repeat visits (data at 0 RTT, but restricted to idempotent requests due to replay risk).

flashcards.q: Why is 0-RTT data in QUIC unsafe for a POST/write?
flashcards.a: The first-flight 0-RTT data can be replayed by an attacker who captured it, since there's no fresh handshake proof yet -- safe only for idempotent/safe-to-duplicate operations, not for payments or other writes.

flashcards.q: How does a client discover a server supports HTTP/3, given QUIC has no ALPN-equivalent bootstrap?
flashcards.a: The server advertises `Alt-Svc: h3=":443"` in a response header over an existing HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2 (TCP) connection; the client caches this and tries QUIC directly on the next visit, since ALPN itself requires an existing TLS/TCP handshake to negotiate over.

flashcards.q: Why does gRPC require HTTP/2, and is domain sharding still a good idea under HTTP/2/3?
flashcards.a: gRPC needs independent multiplexed streams and true bidirectional streaming, which HTTP/1.1 has no concept of. Domain sharding is now counterproductive: it fragments HPACK's shared dynamic table and forces multiple handshakes/slow-starts that a single multiplexed connection was designed to avoid.
